zh:
卷第七
隋天台智者大師說
弟子法慎記
弟子灌頂再治
釋禪波羅蜜修證第七之三（修證亦有漏亦無漏禪）
今約三種法門以辯亦有漏亦無漏禪：一者、六妙門；二者、十六特勝；三者、通明觀。此三法門亦得說為淨禪。此中明淨禪與《阿毘曇》有小異，淺深、位次，並如前第五卷中說，但教門分一息道，立三種禪，為化眾生。
en:
Fascicle Seven
Spoken by the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, of the Sui dynasty
Recorded by his disciple Fashen
Revised and edited by his disciple Guanding
Explaining Dhyāna-Pāramitā's Cultivation and Realization, Topic 7, Part 3 (Cultivating and Realizing Dhyāna That Is Both Contaminated and Uncontaminated)

Here, with reference to three dharma-gates, dhyāna that is both contaminated and uncontaminated is now distinguished: the six wondrous gates; the sixteen special excellences; and the thorough-and-bright contemplation. These three dharma-gates may also be spoken of as the pure dhyānas. What is clarified here regarding the pure dhyānas differs slightly from the Abhidharma's own account; their shallowness, depth, and sequence of stages are all as already given in fascicle 5 above — it is simply that the teaching divides the single path of the breath, establishing three kinds of dhyāna, for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

zh: 今須略推此教意，多是對三種人根性不同：一者、自有眾生慧性多而定性少，為說六妙門。六妙門中慧性多故，於欲界初禪中即能發無漏，此未必至上地諸禪也。二者、自有眾生定根多而慧性少，為說十六特勝。慧根性少故，下地不即發無漏；定性多故，以具上地諸禪，方得修道。三者、自有眾生定慧根性等，為說通明。通明者，亦具根本禪，而觀慧巧細，從於下地乃至上地皆能發無漏也。此是隨機之說。若隨對治，則與此相違，如前五門中意可解。
en: Here, the intent behind this teaching should be briefly reasoned through: it is, for the most part, matched to three kinds of person, differing in capacity. First, there are sentient beings whose wisdom-nature is abundant while their concentration-nature is slight — for these, the six wondrous gates are taught. Within the six wondrous gates, because wisdom-nature is abundant, one is able to bring forth the uncontaminated already within the desire realm or the first dhyāna — this need not wait until reaching the dhyānas of the higher stages at all.

Second, there are sentient beings whose faculty of concentration is abundant while their wisdom-nature is slight — for these, the sixteen special excellences are taught. Because the faculty of wisdom is slight, the lower stages do not immediately bring forth the uncontaminated; because the nature of concentration is abundant, only once complete in the dhyānas of the higher stages is the path actually cultivated.

Third, there are sentient beings whose faculties of concentration and wisdom are equal — for these, the thorough-and-bright contemplation is taught. As for the thorough-and-bright contemplation: this, too, is complete with the root dhyānas, but its contemplative wisdom is skillful and fine, able to bring forth the uncontaminated from the lower stage all the way through the higher stage alike. This is a teaching given according to capacity. Were it instead given according to the antidote, it would run contrary to this — the sense of this may be understood from the five gates already discussed above.

This opening finally cashes out a promise this treatise has been making since fascicle 1 — the six wondrous gates, the sixteen special excellences, and the thorough-and-bright contemplation have all been named repeatedly as attainments along the way, but never given their own full treatment until now. The three-way matching to practitioner capacity (wisdom-heavy, concentration-heavy, or balanced) is a genuinely practical piece of pedagogy: rather than one universal curriculum, the treatise offers three different entry points into the identical underlying territory, each suited to the balance of faculties a student already has. The text itself labels this a teaching "according to capacity," adding that a teaching given according to the antidote would run the other way.

items.en: The Six Wondrous Gates: Name and Sequence
items.zh: 六妙門 · 釋名、辨位次

zh: 初釋六妙門，為三：一者、釋名；二、辨位次；三、明修證。第一、釋名者，所言六妙門者：一、數；二、隨；三、止；四、觀；五、還；六、淨。通稱六妙門者，妙名涅槃，此之妙法能通至涅槃，故名妙門，亦名六妙門。此六妙門，三是定法，三是慧法。定愛慧策，亦有漏亦無漏，義在於此。
en: First, explaining the six wondrous gates: this is given in three parts — explaining the name; distinguishing their sequence of stages; and clarifying their cultivation and realization.

First, explaining the name: as for what is called the six wondrous gates, these are: counting; following; stilling; contemplating; returning; and purifying. As for why they are called, in general, the six wondrous gates: "wondrous" names nirvāṇa — this wondrous dharma is able to lead through all the way to nirvāṇa, and so is named the wondrous gate, also called the six wondrous gates. Of these six wondrous gates, three are dharmas of concentration, and three are dharmas of wisdom. Concentration brings attachment and wisdom spurs onward — this is precisely the sense in which they are both contaminated and uncontaminated at once.

zh: 二、辨次位者，此六妙門位即無定。所以者何？若於欲界、未到地中巧行六法，第六淨心成就，即發三乘無漏，況復進得上地諸禪而不疾證道。雖此與前有異，是以《瑞應經》云：「因此六法，遊止三四，出生十二。」此而推之，故知此六妙門位則不必定耳。
en: Second, distinguishing their sequence of stages: the stages of these six wondrous gates are not fixed at all. Why is this? If, within the desire realm or the "not-yet-arrived" state, these six dharmas are skillfully practiced, and the sixth, purity of mind, is brought to completion, the uncontaminated attainment of the three vehicles is thereby brought forth directly — how much more, then, could one who goes on to attain the dhyānas of the higher stages fail to realize the path all the more quickly? Although this differs somewhat from what was given before, the Sūtra of Auspicious Manifestations accordingly says: "Through these six dharmas, roaming and abiding through the third and fourth dhyānas, twelve are brought forth." Reasoning this through, it is thus known that the sequence of stages for these six wondrous gates is not fixed at all.

The three-and-three split (counting, following, and stilling as concentration; contemplating, returning, and purifying as wisdom) gives structural shape to a sequence that otherwise reads as a single continuous refinement — the first half quiets the mind, the second half turns that quiet mind reflectively on itself. That the six gates' own stages are explicitly "not fixed," able to bring forth full uncontaminated realization already within the desire realm without ever needing to climb through the higher dhyānas, is the payoff for the "wisdom-heavy" practitioner this method was matched to at the fascicle's opening — depth of insight substituting for depth of concentration.

items.en: The Six Wondrous Gates: Cultivation and Realization

zh: 三、明修證者，若廣明此六法修證，則諸禪皆屬六妙門攝。今但取次第相生入道之正要，以明六妙修證之相。今明修證六妙門，開為十二門也。所以者何？如數有二種：一者、修數；二者、數相應。乃至修淨與相應亦如是。今約修證分別，有十二門：一、修數；二、與數相應。一者、修數。行者調和氣息，不澁不滑，安詳徐數，從一至十，攝心在數，不令馳散，是名修數。二、與數相應者，覺心任運，從一至十，不加功力，心息自住。息既虛凝，心相漸細，患數為麁，意不欲數，爾時行者應當放數修隨。
en: Third, clarifying their cultivation and realization: were the cultivation and realization of these six dharmas explained in full, every dhyāna whatsoever would fall under the six wondrous gates' own scope. Here, only the proper essentials of entering the path through their own sequential arising, one from another, are taken up, in order to clarify the mark of the six wondrous gates' cultivation and realization. Here, clarifying the cultivation and realization of the six wondrous gates, this opens into twelve gates. Why is this? Just as counting itself is of two kinds — cultivating counting, and correspondence with counting — the same holds all the way through cultivating purity and correspondence with purity as well. Here, distinguished with reference to cultivation and realization, there are twelve gates:

First, cultivating counting: the practitioner regulates and harmonizes the breath, neither too rough nor too smooth, counting calmly and slowly, from one to ten, the mind gathered in upon the count, not letting it run off and scatter — this is named cultivating counting.

Second, correspondence with counting: one becomes aware that the mind now proceeds of its own accord, from one to ten, without any further application of effort, mind and breath naturally settled. The breath having grown faint and fixed, the mark of the mind grows gradually finer, troubled now by counting itself as too coarse, the mind no longer wishing to count — at this point, the practitioner should set counting aside and cultivate following instead.

zh: 隨亦有二種：一者、修隨；二者、與隨相應。修隨者，捨數法，一心依隨息之出入，心住息緣，無分散意，是名修隨。二者、與隨相應，心既漸細，覺息長短，遍身入出息，任運相依，意慮怡然凝靜，是名與隨相應。覺隨為麁，心厭欲捨，如人疲極欲眠，不樂眾務，爾時行者應當捨隨修止。
en: Following, too, is of two kinds: cultivating following; and correspondence with following. Cultivating following: relinquishing the method of counting, fixing the mind single-mindedly on the breath's own going out and coming in, the mind abiding on the breath as its object, with no thought of scattering at all — this is named cultivating following. Second, correspondence with following: the mind now grows gradually finer, aware of the breath's own length and shortness, the in-breath and out-breath pervading the whole body, following it spontaneously of its own accord, thought and deliberation content and fixed in stillness — this is named correspondence with following. Aware now that following itself is too coarse, the mind grows weary of it and wishes to relinquish it, like a person utterly exhausted, wishing only to sleep, taking no delight in any further activity — at this point, the practitioner should relinquish following and cultivate stilling instead.

zh: 止有二種：一者、修止；二、與止相應。修止者，三止之中，但用制心止也。制心息諸緣慮，不念數隨，凝靜其心，是名修止。二、與止相應者，自覺身心泯然入定，不見內外相貌，如欲界、未到地等。定法持心，任運不動。行者爾時即作是念：「今此三昧雖復寂靜，而無慧方便，不能破壞生死。」復作是念：「今此定者，皆屬因緣，陰、入、界法和合而有，虛誑不實。我今不覺，應須照了。」作是念已，即不著止。
en: Stilling, too, is of two kinds: cultivating stilling; and correspondence with stilling. Cultivating stilling: among the three kinds of stopping, only restraining-the-mind stopping is used here. Restraining the mind brings every object of deliberation to rest, no longer thinking of counting or following, the mind fixed and still — this is named cultivating stilling. Second, correspondence with stilling: one becomes aware, of oneself, that body and mind have grown indistinct, entering concentration, seeing no mark of either what is within or without, as, for example, in desire-realm concentration, the "not-yet-arrived" state, and the like. The dharma of concentration sustains the mind, unmoved of its own accord. The practitioner, at this point, reflects: "Although this samādhi is indeed still, it lacks any skillful means of wisdom, and so is unable to break through birth-and-death." One reflects further: "This very concentration is itself entirely a matter of causes and conditions, the dharma of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements combining together to produce it — deceptive and unreal. I, not yet aware of this, must now illuminate it clearly." Having reflected in this way, one no longer clings to stilling.

Each transition in this sequence follows an identical pattern worth naming explicitly: cultivation of a given gate leads to correspondence with it (the practice becoming spontaneous), and this very spontaneity is what reveals the next gate's own coarseness by comparison — in counting and following, the practitioner does not decide to move on so much as discover that the current gate has already become too coarse to hold the mind's own refinement. The turn out of stilling works differently: it comes not from finding stilling coarse but from deliberately reflecting that it lacks wisdom. That reflection is significant: it is the exact moment concentration alone is recognized as insufficient without wisdom, "unable to break through birth-and-death" no matter how deep — the hinge on which this whole method turns from the three concentration-gates into the three wisdom-gates.

items.en: Three Kinds of Contemplation, and Cultivating Contemplation Itself
parent: The Six Wondrous Gates: Cultivation and Realization

zh: 起觀分別亦有二種：一者、修觀；二者、與觀相應。一、修觀者，觀有三種：一者、慧行觀，觀真之慧；二者、得解觀，即假想觀；三者、實觀，如事而觀也。今此六妙門、十六特勝、通明等，並正用實觀成就，然後用慧行觀觀理入道。所以者何？名實者，如眾生一期果報，實有四大，不淨三十六物所成，但以無明覆蔽，心眼不開明，則不依實而見。若能審諦觀察，心眼開明，依實而見，故名實慧行觀。及得解觀，在下四諦、十二因緣、九想、背捨等中，當廣分別。
en: Giving rise to contemplation and discrimination is likewise of two kinds: cultivating contemplation; and correspondence with contemplation.

First, cultivating contemplation: contemplation itself is of three kinds — the contemplation of wisdom-conduct, the wisdom that contemplates the true; the contemplation of understanding attained, that is, contemplation through mental visualization; and true contemplation, contemplating things exactly as they actually are. Here, the six wondrous gates, the sixteen special excellences, the thorough-and-bright contemplation, and the rest, all properly use true contemplation to reach their own accomplishment, and only afterward use the contemplation of wisdom-conduct to contemplate principle and enter the path.

Why is this? As for what is meant by "true": it is like the fact that a sentient being's own single life-span's karmic result is, in truth, made up of the four elements, and of the thirty-six impure substances — it is simply that, covered over by ignorance, the mind's own eye fails to open into clarity, and so one does not see it as it truly is. If one is able to closely and carefully contemplate it, the mind's own eye opens into clarity, and one sees it exactly as it truly is — hence this is named "true." The contemplation of wisdom-conduct and the contemplation of understanding attained will be distinguished at length below, within the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, the nine contemplations, the liberations, and the rest.

zh: 云何修習實觀？行者於定心中以心眼諦觀此身中細微入出息，想如空中風，皮筋骨肉、三十六物如芭蕉不實，內外不淨，甚可厭惡。復觀定中喜樂等受，悉有破壞之相，是苦非樂。又觀定中心識無常生滅，剎那不住，無可著處。復觀定中善惡等法，悉屬因緣，皆無自性。如是觀時，能破四倒，不得人我，定何所依？是名修觀。
en: How does one cultivate true contemplation? The practitioner, within the concentrated mind, closely contemplates, with the mind's own eye, the fine, subtle in-breath and out-breath within this very body, conceiving of it as though it were wind within empty space; the skin, sinews, bones, and flesh, the thirty-six substances, as though a plantain trunk, without any solidity at all, impure both within and without, deeply repugnant. One further contemplates that the sensations of joy, happiness, and the rest present within concentration all carry within them a mark of their own eventual destruction — this is suffering, not happiness. One further contemplates that mind and consciousness, within concentration, are impermanent, arising and ceasing, never remaining still for a single instant, with nothing at all in them to cling to. One further contemplates that the wholesome and unwholesome dharmas present within concentration are, in every case, entirely a matter of causes and conditions, without any nature of their own whatsoever. Contemplating in this way, one is able to break through the four inversions, finding no self or person present at all — on what, then, could concentration possibly depend? This is named cultivating contemplation.

The three-kind taxonomy of contemplation — wisdom-conduct (direct insight into the true), understanding-attained (guided visualization), and true contemplation (seeing what is actually there) — sets up a distinction the treatise says it will develop below: the nine contemplations and the liberations, still to be treated in full, are "understanding-attained" contemplation (deliberately constructed mental images), while what is happening here, seeing the breath and body exactly as they present themselves without any imaginative construction at all, is "true contemplation." The explicit statement that all three of this fascicle's named methods rely on true contemplation first, only later adding wisdom-conduct contemplation to reach principle, gives a methodological key for reading everything that follows in both the six wondrous gates and the sixteen special excellences.

quiz.q: With reference to which three dharma-gates is dhyāna both contaminated and uncontaminated distinguished?
options: the four dhyānas, immeasurable minds, formless concentrations
the liberations, stations of mastery, totality-bases
the six wondrous gates, the sixteen special excellences, the thorough-and-bright contemplation
the nine contemplations, eight recollections, ten contemplations
quiz.why: The three gates are the six wondrous gates, the sixteen special excellences, and the thorough-and-bright contemplation, also called the pure dhyānas. Option B is the mundane dhyāna of earlier fascicles.

quiz.q: The teaching divides the single path of the breath into three kinds of dhyāna. For what purpose?
options: for the sake of transforming sentient beings
quiz.why: Their depth and stages are as in fascicle five; the teaching simply divides the one path of the breath into three dhyānas to transform beings of differing capacities.

quiz.q: For beings of what disposition are the six wondrous gates taught?
quiz.why: Beings with abundant wisdom and slight concentration are taught the six wondrous gates, and can bring forth the uncontaminated already in the desire realm or first dhyāna.

quiz.q: Why must practitioners of the sixteen special excellences be complete in the higher dhyānas before cultivating the path?
options: they exist only in the formless realm
wisdom is slight, so the lower stages do not immediately yield the uncontaminated; concentration is abundant, so the path comes after the higher dhyānas
quiz.why: Wisdom being slight, the lower stages do not immediately bring forth the uncontaminated; concentration being abundant, the path is cultivated once the higher dhyānas are complete.

quiz.q: What marks the thorough-and-bright contemplation, and what happens if the teaching follows the antidote instead of capacity?
options: it has the root dhyānas with skillful, fine wisdom, bringing forth the uncontaminated at every stage; following the antidote would run contrary
quiz.why: The thorough-and-bright contemplation has the root dhyānas yet fine contemplative wisdom, bringing forth the uncontaminated from lower to higher stages. This is a teaching by capacity; by antidote it would run contrary.

quiz.q: What are the six wondrous gates, in order?
options: stilling, contemplating, counting, following, returning, purifying
counting, following, stilling, contemplating, returning, purifying
counting, following, contemplating, stilling, returning, purifying
counting, stilling, following, contemplating, purifying, returning
quiz.why: The six are counting, following, stilling, contemplating, returning, and purifying.

quiz.q: What does "wondrous" in "wondrous gate" name?
options: "wondrous" names nirvāṇa; this dharma leads to nirvāṇa, hence the wondrous gate
quiz.why: "Wondrous" names nirvāṇa, and this dharma leads through to nirvāṇa, so it is called the wondrous gate.

quiz.q: How are the six divided into concentration and wisdom, and where lies the sense of "both contaminated and uncontaminated"?
options: three are concentration, three wisdom; concentration attaches and wisdom spurs, and the sense lies there
quiz.why: Three are concentration (counting, following, stilling) and three are wisdom (contemplating, returning, purifying); concentration attaches and wisdom spurs, hence both contaminated and uncontaminated.

quiz.q: Why does the text say the stages of the six wondrous gates are not fixed?
options: practiced skillfully even in the desire realm or not-yet-arrived state, purity of mind brings forth the uncontaminated of the three vehicles
quiz.why: Practiced skillfully in the desire realm or not-yet-arrived state, the sixth gate, purity of mind, already brings forth the uncontaminated of the three vehicles, so the stages are not fixed.

quiz.q: Why do the six wondrous gates open into twelve gates?
options: each has two kinds, cultivating it and corresponding with it
quiz.why: Counting has two kinds, cultivating counting and corresponding with counting, and likewise through purifying, giving twelve gates.

quiz.q: What is the method of cultivating counting?
options: regulate the breath, neither rough nor smooth, count calmly from one to ten, gathering the mind on the count
quiz.why: One regulates the breath, neither rough nor smooth, and counts calmly from one to ten, keeping the mind on the count.

quiz.q: When should one set counting aside and cultivate following?
options: after correspondence with counting, the breath faint and mind finer, one finds counting coarse and no longer wishes to count
quiz.why: When the breath grows faint and the mind finer, counting feels coarse and one no longer wishes to count; then one sets it aside for following.

quiz.q: What is cultivating following?
options: relinquishing counting, following the breath's going out and coming in, the mind abiding on the breath
quiz.why: One relinquishes counting and single-mindedly follows the breath's going out and coming in, the mind abiding on it without scattering.

quiz.q: When following itself feels coarse and one wishes to relinquish it, what comparison is given?
options: like an exhausted person wishing only to sleep, taking no delight in activity
quiz.why: Like an utterly exhausted person who wants only to sleep; then one relinquishes following and cultivates stilling. The gatekeeper appears later, in the special excellences.

quiz.q: Among the three kinds of stopping, which is used in cultivating stilling?
quiz.why: Only restraining-the-mind stopping is used: restraining the mind brings deliberation to rest, no longer thinking of counting or following.

quiz.q: After corresponding with stilling, why does the practitioner no longer cling to it?
options: this samādhi, though still, lacks wisdom to break birth and death, and is produced by conditions, deceptive and unreal
quiz.why: The samādhi lacks the skillful means of wisdom to break birth and death, and is itself produced by conditions, deceptive and unreal; so one no longer clings to it.

quiz.q: Contemplation has three kinds. Which pairing is correct?
options: wisdom-conduct contemplates the true; understanding attained is visualization; true contemplation sees things as they are
understanding attained sees things as they are
quiz.why: The contemplation of wisdom-conduct is wisdom contemplating the true; that of understanding attained is visualization; true contemplation sees things as they actually are.

quiz.q: Which contemplation do the six gates, special excellences, and thorough-and-bright mainly use, and how do they then enter the path?
options: they accomplish themselves through true contemplation, then use wisdom-conduct to contemplate principle and enter the path
quiz.why: They are accomplished through true contemplation and then enter the path by contemplating principle with wisdom-conduct. Understanding attained is discussed later with the nine contemplations and liberations.

quiz.q: In true contemplation, how is the breath conceived, and how are the thirty-six substances seen?
options: breath as diamond, body as mirror
breath as water, body as mountain
the breath as wind in empty space; the thirty-six substances as a plantain trunk without solidity, impure within and without
quiz.why: The subtle breath is conceived as wind in space; the skin, sinews, bones, flesh, and thirty-six substances as a hollow plantain, impure within and without.

quiz.q: In cultivating contemplation, how are the four kinds of things within concentration seen?
options: body impure; joy and happiness as suffering; mind impermanent; dharmas without self-nature
quiz.why: One sees the body as impure, sensations as suffering, mind as impermanent, and dharmas as without self-nature, which breaks the four inversions listed in C.

quiz.q: After breaking the four inversions, with what rhetorical question does the text conclude cultivating contemplation?
options: finding no self or person, on what could concentration depend?
quiz.why: Finding no self or person, on what could concentration depend? "From where does mind arise" belongs to returning.
